https://www.dw.com/en/13-killed-in-touri.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I8WM The Nazca Lines in southern Peru are a UNESCO World Heritage Site [FILE] Image: Imago/S. spiegl Advertisement A small plane carrying tourists to see Peru 's famed Nazca Lines archaeological site crashed, killing all 13 people on board, authorities in Nazca province said on Saturday. "We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died," said Police Major Jorge Andrade at the crash site in southern Peru. Andrade also said that "given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors," adding that four bodies have been recovered so far. Peru's local news site RPP reported that seven Italians, two Germans and two Spaniards were killed in the accident. There's no official confirmation about the nationalities of those aboard the plane. The plane crashed shortly after 1:00 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) after taking off from the airport in the city of Pisco, located about 240 kilometers (150 miles) south of the capital, Lima. What else do we know about the crash in the Peruvian desert? ​RPP reported that the small plane lost contact with the control tower minutes after takeoff. The crash occurred in the area of Pueblo Viejo, about six kilometers from the city of Nazca and ​around 12 kilometers from the Nazca Lines site , according to local authorities. Nazca's government said the plane was operated by local Peruvian company Aerodiana. The airline was not immediately available for comment. However, on its website, Aerodiana says it has operated scenic flights over the Nazca lines for the last 14 years. The reasons behind the plane crash are still unknown. Peruvian authorities said the incident is under investigation. Tourist planes over Nazca Lines have crashed before too Stretching across the desert near the city of Nazca, the Nazca Lines are a vast collection of geoglyphs created hundreds of years ago by Peru's Indigenous inhabitants. The famous desert geoglyphs, many depicting animals, can only be fully appreciated from the air or elevated viewing platforms. The latest incident is not the first plane to crash near the site in recent decades. In 2022, a plane crash killed seven people on board , including two Chileans and three Dutch nationals. In 2010, another fatal crash killed four British tourists and two Peruvian crew members. Storms have worsened conditions for hundreds of thousands of Palestinians living in temporary accommodation. Photograph: Hassan al-Jedi/APAImages/Shutterstock Global development Thousands without shelter face lethal conditions in storm-hit Gaza as they wait for 150,000 tents Charities warn of lack of protection amid health fears for more than 940,000 displaced people living in flood-prone areas Supported by About this content Kaamil Ahmed Wed 11 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 00.03 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms at the weekend, while 150,000 new shelters are held outside Gaza awaiting Israeli approval to enter, aid agencies have said. At least four Palestinian children and woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents. Thousands have been left without shelter and sanitation infrastructure has been destroyed, with sewage spewing into people’s tents. “All our clothes were soaked. My kids are all sick and I can’t afford to buy them more clothes,” said Raed Jamal, a displaced Palestinian. “Watching them suffering in the cold is heartbreaking.” Storm winds rattles tents for displaced Palestinians on Gaza’s coast “These conditions are so difficult, the whole night I had to use pots to collect rainwater because it was falling on us.” He shared videos with the Guardian of his tent shaking in the wind as rain poured through holes in its roof. Aid workers warn disease will spread rapidly unless families are quickly supplied with new shelters and ways to keep warm. View image in fullscreen Displaced Palestinians repair storm-damaged tents in western Gaza City last week. Photograph: Mohammed Salha/APAImages/Shutterstock The UK-based charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said it was concerned about a rise in health problems because families were living in flooded tents with nowhere else to go. “Our medical teams expect to see more respiratory illnesses and other health complications linked to cold, damp and overcrowded conditions, and we fear more children could die from hypothermia, as happened last winter,” said Mai Elawawda, MAP’s communications officer in Gaza . According to the UN, 940,000 people in Gaza are in areas at risk of flooding in makeshift tents without protection from heavy rainfall. The flooding threat has been heightened as facilities for pumping out storm water are not operating due to a lack of power. Shelterbox, a charity working in humanitarian crisis zones, said the tents it usually supplies during emergencies have been waiting outside Gaza for almost two years and it has instead been forced to improvise shelters built from tarpaulins and wooden pallets. But even these materials, it says, are being restricted. “The latest devastating floods impacting displaced people in Gaza demonstrate exactly why more durable improvements to shelter are desperately needed ahead of winter,” said a Shelterbox spokesperson. “The over-reliance on emergency solutions, rather than building shelters from more robust materials, means that many people are living in shelters that are simply not suitable to withstand the weather conditions that the region experiences and will quickly deteriorate.” View image in fullscreen Palestinians inspect tents buried under rocks and earth a day after a large sandstone slab collapsed at a displacement camp, killing at least five people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP A child drowned in flood waters and at least three children and their mother died when a sand dune fell on their tent at the weekend, according to the Palestinian health ministry. The UN said 26,000 households had sought its help after the rains and at least 3,900 households were now without shelter at all. Palestinians in Gaza are facing their second winter since a ceasefire was agreed more than a year ago, but aid workers said conditions were no better than last year because of Israeli restrictions on “dual-use items” and backlogs at crossings were limiting critical supplies to build shelters . “It’s very difficult to deal with it because there’s also there’s no clear process for things. There’s a level of capriciousness that one day toolkits will be allowed in, another day toolkits will not and they don’t say why,” said Sheltherbox the spokesperson. The Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu) has called on the British government to pressure Israel to allow supplies into Gaza and reverse restrictions on humanitarian workers, including restoring the licences of dozens of organisations, such as Médecins Sans Frontières, Oxfam and the Norwegian Refugee Council. View image in fullscreen Employees and workers of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) hold placards during a protest in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, 9 November. Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock “The predictable winter rains and floods have, as warned about, battered already devastated Palestinians, where disease and malnutrition is rife, and a basic tent blocked by Israel is a manmade and political scarcity,” said Caabu’s head of parliamentary affairs, Joseph Willits. “A lack of political action isn’t something a Palestinian family trying to shelter from Gaza’s floods can afford.” Israel claimed last week to have allowed 10,000 tents into Gaza, but that falls far short of the number needed – the UN said 150,000 were waiting outside Gaza for entry for the estimated 94% of Palestinians in Gaza who need help finding shelter. The Israeli NGO Gisha, which lobbies for goods and people to be able to enter and exit Gaza more freely, said the Israeli authorities had enforced stricter limits on goods entering Gaza than in previous ceasefires. A Palestinian child shows the inside of his family’s tent during a storm in Gaza While the Israeli authorities claim to be allowing an average of 600 trucks into Gaza each day, they count 12 pallets of goods as a single truck, even though a truck usually carries about 20 pallets – which could amount to about a 40% reduction on what could be carried into Gaza. Gisha has also accused Israeli authorities of a lack of transparency on what is being allowed to enter Gaza. Nour al-Batsh , the mother of a seven-month-old child, said she was forced to rent a partially destroyed apartment she shares with others for $500 a month, relying on donations from abroad, after her tent collapsed. “The cold is lethal. Living in a tent by the sea means facing the constant threat of death from the freezing temperatures,” said Batsh, who can see her old tent from her current shelter. “We are still in autumn, and winter has not even properly begun. I look at my fragile tent and I beg God that I will not have to go back to it. Because death inside that tent is certain.” Explore more on these topics Global development Gaza Internally displaced people Palestine Israel-Gaza war Humanitarian response Israel news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
